title: Annona senegalensis

{{short description|Species of plant}} {{Speciesbox |image = Annona senegalensis (4337693176).jpg |image_caption = ''Annona senegalensis'' fruit on a stem, with leaves near [[Fada N'gourma]] in [[Burkina Faso]]. |status = LC |status_system = IUCN3.1 |status_ref = {{cite iucn |author=Botanic Gardens Conservation International (BGCI). |author2=IUCN SSC Global Tree Specialist Group |date=2019 |title=''Annona senegalensis'' |volume=2019 |article-number=e.T136996621A146212025 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2019-2.RLTS.T136996621A146212025.en |access-date=20 November 2021}} |genus = Annona |species = senegalensis |authority = [[Christiaan Hendrik Persoon|Pers.]] ''A. senegalensis'' was originally described and published in ''Synopsis Plantarum'' 2(1): 95. 1806. }} '''''Annona senegalensis''''', commonly known as '''African custard-apple''',{{cite book|author=National Research Council|title=Lost Crops of Africa: Volume III: Fruits|volume=3|date=2008-01-25|publisher=National Academies Press|isbn=978-0-309-10596-5|chapter=Custard Apples|chapter-url=http://books.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=11879&page=243}} '''wild custard apple''', '''wild soursop''', '''abo ibobo''' ([[Yoruba language]]),{{cite journal|title=Yoruba Food|first=William R.|last=Bascom|date=Jan 1951|journal=Africa|publisher=Cambridge University Press|volume=20|issue=1|page=47|doi=10.2307/1156157|jstor=1156157 |s2cid=149837516 }} '''{{Transliteration|mnk|italic=no|sunkungo}}''' ([[Mandinka language]]), '''Gwandan daji''' ([[Hausa language]]) and '''{{Transliteration|wo|italic=no|dorgot}}''' ([[Wolof language]]){{cite book |last1=Jones |first1=Michael |title=Flowering plants of the Gambia |date=1994 |publisher=A.A. Balkema |isbn=90-5410-197-0 |page=19}} is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the custard apple family, [[Annonaceae]]. The specific epithet, ''senegalensis'', translates to mean "of Senegal", the country where the [[type (biology)|type]] specimen was collected.{{cite web|url=http://www.worldagroforestrycentre.org/sea/Products/AFDbases/af/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=213|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130416043642/http://www.worldagroforestrycentre.org/sea/Products/AFDbases/af/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=213|archive-date=April 16, 2013|title=Annona senegalensis|work=AgroForestry Tree Database|access-date=August 3, 2010}} A traditional food plant in [[Africa]], the fruits of ''A. senegalensis'' have the potential to improve nutrition, boost [[food security]], foster [[rural development]] and support [[sustainable agriculture|sustainable land care]]. Well known where it grows naturally, it is largely unheard of elsewhere. ==Description== ''Annona senegalensis'' takes the form of either a [[shrub]] or small [[tree]], growing between two and six meters tall. Occasionally, it may become as tall as 11 m. *It has [[Bark (botany)|bark]] of smooth or coarse texture, that can be a gray-silver or gray-brown. It is leaf-scarred, with nearly round flaking, showing lighter-hued spaces of under bark. *[[Branch]]es have thick, gray, brown or yellow tomentum when new, but this is later shed with age. *Its green to blue-green [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, simple, oblong to ovate to elliptic, from 6–18.5 long by 2.5–11.5 cm wide, with upper sides nearly hairless, but often hairy on the undersides, green to reddish, aracnose veins on both surfaces, with rounded to slightly notched apices. The leaf base is squared or barely lobeliar. The leaf margin is entire. Stout petioles are 0.5–2.5 cm long. *[[Flower]]s mature to up to 3 cm in diameter, on 2 cm stalks, either singular, or two to four, ascending from the leaf axils. Six thick, creamy or xanthate petals display in double whorls, and green on the outside, but either creamy or sanguine within; each is roughly {{convert|0.8|–|1.5|by|0.9|–|1.1|cm}}, hairless or somewhat fuzzy. Petals' inner whorls curve over its stamens and ovary, three loose sepals are ovalish, and smaller than the petals (3–4 by 4–5 mm). The stamens range from {{convert|1.7|to|2.5|mm}} long. The plant flowers from approximately April through June. *Its [[pollen]] is shed as permanent tetrads.Walker JW (1971) Pollen Morphology, Phytogeography, and Phylogeny of the Annonaceae. Contributions from the Gray Herbarium of Harvard University, 202: 1-130. *[[Fruit]]s are formed of numerous fused, fleshy, bumpy, ovaform or globular carpels about {{convert|2.5|–|5|by|2.5–4|cm}}. They are green when young, ripening to yellow, and eventually to orange, packed with many burnt-orange-colored, oblong, cylindrical [[seed]]s. The fruit stalk is {{convert|1.5|–|5|cm}} long. ''A. senegalensis'' is generally [[pollination|pollinated]] by several species of [[beetle]], but can be hand pollinated when grown as a [[crop|crop plant]]. Its seed viability usually lasts no more than six months. ==Habitat== ''A. senegalensis'' tends to grow in semiarid to subhumid regions adjacent to the coast, often, but not exclusively, on [[coral]]-based rocks with mostly [[sand]]y, [[loam]]y [[soil]]s, from sea level up to 2400 meters, at [[arithmetic mean|mean]] temperatures between 17 and 30 °C, and mean [[rain]]fall between {{convert|700|and|2500|mm}}. They are often solitary plants within [[woodland savannah]] [[understory]], also frequently in [[swamp|swamp forest]]s, or [[bank (geography)|riverbank]]s, or on former [[farm|cropland]] left [[crop rotation|fallow]] for an extended period. ==Distribution== ''A. senegalensis'' is native to tropical east and northeast, west and west-central, and southern Africa, as well as southern subtropical Africa, and islands in the western [[Indian Ocean]]. Within the nation of [[South Africa]], it is found in [[KwaZulu-Natal]], [[Limpopo]], and [[Mpumalanga]]. In Zimbabwe it is widespread in the [[Bikita]] district. ''A. senegalensis'' has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in parts of [[India]]. It is also found in the islands of Maldives. ==Uses== {{more medical citations needed|section|date=September 2017}} The primary use of this plant is for food, but it has applications in numerous aspects of human endeavor, and every part of the plant has properties and uses. The flowers, leaves and fruit are edible and culinary: white fruit [[pulp (fruit)|pulp]] has a mild, [[pineapple]]-like flavor. Flowers are added to spice or garnish meals; leaves are eaten by humans as vegetables, or grazed by [[livestock]]. Leaves are also part of the diet of the [[West African giraffe]].{{cite web|url=http://ne.chm-cbd.net/biodiversity/aires-prot/le-sanctuaire-des-girafes|title=Le Sanctuaire des Girafes|author=Mariama Galadima|publisher=Centre d'Echange d'Informations sur la Biodiversité du Niger|language=fr|date=July 7, 2008|access-date=April 25, 2019|archive-date=December 17, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191217151713/http://ne.chm-cbd.net/biodiversity/aires-prot/le-sanctuaire-des-girafes/}} The leaves are also used to create a [[Herbal tonic|general health tonic]], in the treatment of [[pneumonia]], and as [[mattress]] and [[pillow]] stuffing. Specific to [[Sudan]], leaves are boiled in the making of [[perfume]]. Bark can be processed to produce yellow-brown [[dye]], [[insecticide]], or medicine for treating a wide array of ailments, including [[worm]]s [[parasitism|parasitic]] on the [[intestines]] or flesh (notably [[Dracunculiasis|guinea worm]]s), [[diarrhea]], [[gastroenteritis]], [[respiratory tract infection|lung infection]]s, [[toothache]]s, and even [[snakebite]]s. [[Natural gum]] in the bark is used to close open wounds. [[Root]]s are also used medicinally in treating a gamut of conditions, from [[dizziness]] and [[dyspepsia|indigestion]] to chest colds to [[sexually transmitted disease|venereal disease]]s. [[Basal shoot|Suckering shoot]]s provide binding [[natural fiber|fiber]]s, and the malleable, pale brown to white [[wood]] is used to [[woodworking|carve tool handle]]s, or fashioned into poles. [[Wood ash]] is an admixture to [[chewing tobacco]] and [[Snuff (tobacco)|snuff]], and also in [[soap]] production as [[solvent]]. The [[essential oil]]s in the fruits and leaves are valued for their [[organic chemistry|organic chemical]] constituents: [[car-3-ene]] (in fruit) and [[linalool]] (from leaves). Certain parts of ''A. senegalensis'' are used in treating [[dermatology|skin]] or [[ophthalmology|eye disorder]]s. Many South Africans believe the roots can cure [[insanity]]. Some [[Mozambique|Mozambican]]s feed them to infants to [[weaning|wean]] them from their [[breastfeeding|mother's breast]]. ==Anthracnose== Like other species within the genus ''Anonna'', ''A. senegalensis'' is commonly afflicted by [[anthracnose]], brought on by the [[pathogen#Fungi|fungal pathogen]] ''[[Colletotrichum|Colletotrichum gloesporioides]]'', which leads to leaf drop, eventually followed by [[Natural mummy|mummification]] of its fruit. Controls often employed against the disease include spray applications of [[fermate]] or [[Dichlone|Phygon]]. ==References== {{Reflist|colwidth=26em}} ==External links== {{commons category|Annona senegalensis|
